items.stem: An internal tool drafts email replies for a team's private queue, with no user-facing output and no tools; the security team wants every internal tool wrapped in the same four-layer template before allocating review budget. Which control set fits this tool's risk?

opts.t: Scope the tool's actions narrowly and require human approval before any tool call executes.
Add detailed logging of every draft so the team can review usage patterns afterward.
Add a system-prompt instruction asking the model to flag any draft it is unsure about.
Keep input validation and an output schema check; skip tool scoping and human approval, since neither applies here.

items.whyRight: Guardrail layers are matched to consequence: this tool has no external output and no tools for anything to scope or gate, so input validation and an output schema check are the only layers with something real to check, and adding permission scoping or human approval would cover nothing.

whyWrong.A: The stem states the tool holds no tools; there is no tool call to gate and nothing to scope, so this control has nothing to act on.
whyWrong.B: Logging records what the tool already did; it does not decide which boundary control this low-consequence tool actually needs.
whyWrong.C: A prompt instruction depends on the model behaving as asked; it is a tendency standing in for the deterministic check the boundary needs.

items.t1Clause: with no user-facing output and no tools
items.factAnswerRaw: Input validation and output schema checks are sufficient

items.stem: A support bot handling thousands of chats daily stopped referencing anything said two turns earlier, after the team switched to a lighter client library that trims payloads; conversations run four or five turns, and the model version is unchanged. What should the team check first?

opts.t: Confirm the application is resending the full conversation history with each request.
Increase the context window setting so more prior turns fit in each call.
Roll back to the previous model version to rule out a degraded release.
Add a system-prompt reminder telling the assistant to remember what the user said earlier.

items.whyRight: Losing reference to something said two turns back in a short conversation is a classic missing-history symptom, not a capacity limit; the model version is pinned and unchanged, so the first check is whether the calling application still sends the full turn history with each request.

whyWrong.B: The conversation is only four or five turns; that is far below any context limit, so the stem's own evidence rules out a capacity explanation.
whyWrong.C: The model version is stated as unchanged; chasing a version rollback discards a component that was never implicated instead of checking what actually changed.
whyWrong.D: Telling the assistant to remember does nothing if the earlier turn's text was never sent back to it; the instruction cannot act on data the request never contained.

items.stem: A claims team can sustainably staff review of only 5% of daily volume, and every high-value claim must be checked regardless of model confidence. It proposes reviewing everything at launch and relaxing the rate once trust in the model grows. What replaces this plan?

opts.t: Review every claim at launch and lower the review rate as trust in the model grows.
Auto-approve high-confidence, low-value claims; send every high-value claim to review regardless of confidence; audit the approved stream on a schedule.
Randomly sample a fixed slice of all claims for review, sized to match the team's staffing capacity.
Let the model flag any claim it reports being unsure about, and send only those to review.

items.whyRight: Blanket review is a staffing collapse from day one, not a temporary starting point, since no exit criterion is stated; routing on confidence and consequence together lets low-value, high-confidence claims clear immediately while every high-value claim still reaches a reviewer.

whyWrong.A: Reviewing everything from launch already exceeds the stated 5% staffing capacity, and no threshold or date is named for when review would relax.
whyWrong.C: A fixed sample sized to staffing capacity is the right way to monitor the auto-approved stream, not the way to decide which claims skip review in the first place.
whyWrong.D: The model's own statement of confidence is not a valid routing signal; a fluent model can be equally sure when it is wrong as when it is right.

items.t1Clause: can sustainably staff review of only 5% of daily volume

items.stem: Security wants recent request and response traffic preserved long enough to investigate incidents after the fact, while compliance requires that regulated interaction data not be kept beyond a justified, stated purpose. Which retention approach satisfies both requirements at once?

opts.t: Retain only a decision trace (versions, thresholds, outcome) for every interaction, and discard the raw traffic.
Delete all request and response logs immediately after each interaction completes.
Keep a bounded window of traffic, de-identified, under a stated investigation purpose and duration.
Retain all traffic indefinitely, restricted to the security team through role-based permissions.

items.whyRight: A bounded window with a stated investigation purpose and de-identification lets the security team trace recent incidents while capping how long regulated traffic exists, satisfying the retention limit and the operational need with a single design choice rather than trading one for the other.

whyWrong.A: A decision trace records what a rule concluded, not the underlying interaction content; an incident investigation needs the actual traffic, which this discards entirely.
whyWrong.B: Deleting immediately removes anything to investigate after the fact, satisfying the retention limit only by defeating the stated investigative need entirely.
whyWrong.D: Indefinite retention with access controls still leaves regulated traffic stored with no bounded duration or purpose; access control does not shrink the retention exposure.

items.t1Clause: Security wants recent request and response traffic preserved long enough to investigate incidents after the fact
